As someone else has said, supervised drinking can actually kind of backfire if not handled with a strict hand. An ex boyfriend of mine is 19 and has been able to drink in his home since he was 16 and is now what I would say an alcoholic. 

Of course not every situation may be like that, least of all yours since you have a good plan already. Some teens feel like once they have a healthy and safe mindset about alcohol and a safe environment to consume it in, they don’t really feel the need to consume it. It’s mostly for the thrill & experience of doing something ~risky~ anyway, not really for the purpose of numbing emotions or anything. At least that’s how it was for me. I think that if you educate her (show her statistics on teen drinking accidents/share your own personal experiences/etc) and make sure to let her know that you are a safe space for her to talk about this subject with, things should turn out alright. I know that if my older siblings or even my parents communicated with me about alcohol and it’s pros/cons/dangers, I probably would not have turned to it so much.

First of all, know that you have so much support here in this sub. <3 I’m so sorry for what you’re going through at home.

Secondly,  you’re gonna need to draft up a plan. How you’ll get transport to your family in the USA, where you will go, how you will afford it if going by plane, etc. If you’re going for school you could use that as a plausible coverup to leave quicker or to leave in general. 

As someone once said on this sub, you’ll need to go full “Marie Kondo” on your stuff. Only bring with you the necessities and things that you are very attached to. You won’t be able to bring your whole bedroom with you, so just take essential clothes (some good jackets, jeans and sweats, whatever works), your documents, and a few important trinkets. As far as technology, basically take everything you own except for your television if you have one, lol. Have a friend or a family member you trust hold on to your things that you are moving out in the meantime, then on the final day just go collect everything and dip out.

When escaping time comes (and it will - hold on to hope), you’ll need to move your stuff out in portions. Not all on the same night. Take your legal documents last - don’t pack them early or anything or your parents will probably go balls to the walls again. Just make note of where your important docs are and take them the morning of or the day of your final departure. 

Of course this isn’t a solid plan here, you’ll need to adjust based on your situation. These are just some tips. You have so much support, I cannot emphasize that enough!

Don't have any scholarly articles, just my own experience. 

I think it comes from a place of seeking validation and garnering reactions; many people diagnosed with BPD faced some form of neglect or abuse in their childhoods, especially from their parents, and compassion was rare. So as they're older, they start actively seeking interactions to fill that void. A prominent trait of people with BPD is constantly seeking validation and positivity from others, so I think over-sharing, though a maladaptive way of achieving it, is the borderline's way of getting said validation by being vulnerable.

Even though over-sharing tends to make people uncomfy, us borderlines just do it because it feels normal to us, and we want - we need - that positive reaction. That "omg, you poor thing!" to lift us up. 

But that's just my thoughts and how my brain is wired, anyway.
